title: Eton Mess
subtitle: Crushed meringue, strawberries, and whipped cream
excerpt: Broken meringue, macerated strawberries, and softly whipped double cream stirred together into a glorious, casual mess. One of the simplest great British desserts.

recipe.sourceNotes: Eton Mess is named after Eton College, the boarding school in Berkshire, where it has been served at the annual cricket match against Harrow since at least the 1930s. The dish was likely invented accidentally when a pavlova or meringue was dropped or crushed, and a resourceful person simply combined the broken pieces with the cream and fruit and served it anyway. The strawberry is by far the most traditional fruit, in season at the same time as the Eton v Harrow match each June. Good meringue is the key ingredient: homemade is better than shop-bought.

content.text: Macerating the strawberries with a little sugar and lemon juice draws out their juice and deepens their flavour. Whip the cream to soft peaks only: over-whipped cream will be stiff and cloying. Assemble and serve the mess immediately once everything is combined, as the meringue will begin to soften the moment it meets the cream.

items.preparation: made into 8 meringue nests, or use shop-bought

content.text: Toss the quartered strawberries with the caster sugar and lemon juice. Leave to macerate for at least 15 minutes at room temperature.
Whip the double cream with the icing sugar and vanilla to soft, billowing peaks. Stop before the cream becomes stiff.

Break the meringues into large irregular pieces. Reserve a handful of the prettiest strawberry pieces for the top. Fold together the cream, remaining strawberries with all their juice, and the broken meringue. Do not over-mix: streaks and variation are correct. Spoon into glasses or bowls. Top with the reserved strawberries. Serve at once.
